citation: MWAA, "Metropolitan Washington Airports Authority Completes Negotiations for New Use and Lease Agreement with Airlines" (2024), mwaa.com: 15-year agreement effective January 1, 2025; capital construction program of approximately $6.99 billion at IAD and $2.39 billion at DCA — approximately $9 billion together; airline-funded debt-service coverage to at least a 140-percent target ratio. Majority-in-interest thresholds and cost-recovery categorization not verified from primary agreement text.
claim: MWAA holds a committed capital construction program of approximately $6.99 billion at IAD and $2.39 billion at DCA — roughly $9 billion together — under the fifteen-year Airline Use and Lease Agreement
verification_note: MWAA press release fetched and figures confirmed 2026-08-11 ($6.99B IAD, $2.39B DCA, $9B program, 15-year term, 140% coverage target).

citation: July 29, 2026 joint announcement by the President, the U.S. Transportation Secretary, United, and MWAA, as reported in "Inside the $20B+ Plan to Remake Washington Dulles International Airport" (travelagentcentral.com) and *Simple Flying*, "Goodbye Mobile Lounges: Here Comes Washington Dulles' $20+ Billion Revival": more than 5 million square feet of new or refurbished facilities, Concourse C/D replacement, AeroTrain extension, mobile-lounge retirement, preservation of the Saarinen Main Terminal. claim: On July 29, 2026, the President, the U.S. Transportation Secretary, United's CEO, and MWAA jointly announced a Dulles transformation described at more than $20 billion, provisional pending Board action.
verification_note: transportation.gov announcement and MWAA companion release confirmed in fact-check pass.

citation: MWAA Office of Engineering, *Design Manual* (seven volumes, annually updated), mwaa.com; the quoted characterization appears in MWAA's own description. The Manual's current acoustic and PA content, and the reach of tenant technology standards into airline holdroom audio, were not verified from primary Manual text in this research pass.
claim: Every square foot of that work passes through the seven-volume MWAA Design Manual — "a mandatory guide with the force of law on the airport property."
verification_note: Quoted characterization confirmed on MWAA's site in fact-check pass; the Manual's current acoustic/PA content was not verified from primary text, as the footnote states.

citation: MWAA, Concourse E project disclosures (flydulles.com): approximately 435,000 square feet, 14 gates, initial phase opening fall 2026. Verified against the project page August 11, 2026.
claim: Concourse E — approximately 435,000 square feet, fourteen gates, opening this fall — carries the first commissioned intelligibility and ambient baseline under representative traffic.
verification_note: flydulles.com project page fetched 2026-08-11: 435,000 sq ft and 14 gates confirmed; fall 2026 opening corroborated by multiple 2025-2026 press reports.

citation: National Transportation Safety Board, Aircraft Accident Report NTSB/AIR-26/02, *Midair Collision over the Potomac River — PSA Airlines Flight 5342* (final, 2026, ntsb.gov). The January 29, 2025 collision and its 67 fatalities were documented in contemporaneous coverage: CNN, "DCA midair collision first responders, others remembered by victims' families as heroes" (cnn.com).
claim: After the January 29, 2025 midair collision and the NTSB's final report
verification_note: NTSB report identity and date confirmed in fact-check pass (ntsb.gov).

citation: NFPA 72, *National Fire Alarm and Signaling Code*, emergency communications systems intelligibility criteria: STI of at least 0.45 at 90% of measurement locations within each acoustically distinguishable space, average STI of at least 0.50. Primary code is paywalled; figures verified against technical secondary sources reproducing the code language (commercialintegrator.com, "Mass Notification: Intelligibility is NOT Optional") and corroborated across ten-plus records in the research base.
claim: NFPA 72 requires emergency voice systems to achieve a Speech Transmission Index of at least 0.45 at 90% of measurement locations in each acoustically distinguishable space, average 0.50.
verification_note: Primary code paywalled; exact threshold language verified against the technical secondary source reproducing the code text, with the 0.70-CIS conflict resolved in the fact-check report.

citation: Airport Cooperative Research Program, *ACRP Research Report 175: Improving Intelligibility of Airport Terminal Public Address Systems*, Transportation Research Board (2017): recommends a minimum STI of 0.45 and a signal-to-noise ratio of 10 dB(A) for public-address broadcasts in pier-style departure lounges (nap.nationalacademies.org/read/24839).
claim: ACRP Research Report 175 recommends a minimum STI of 0.45 with 10 dB(A) signal-to-noise in pier-style departure lounges;
verification_note: Figures match the ledger record quoting the report's recommendation (nap.nationalacademies.org).

citation: International Electrotechnical Commission, IEC 60268-16:2020, *Sound system equipment — Part 16: Objective rating of speech intelligibility by speech transmission index* (webstore.iec.ch/en/publication/26771): defines the STI model, test signals, and measurement methods. Standard is paywalled; MWAA specifications can require compliance by reference.
claim: IEC 60268-16:2020 defines the Speech Transmission Index model and its measurement methods.
verification_note: IEC webstore listing confirms the standard defines the STI model and measurement methods.

citation: Commercial pricing guides: new-construction acoustic ceiling installation $5–$15 per square foot (designtransitionstudio.com, "Acoustical Ceiling Cost Per Square Foot: Price Guide 2026," which also quotes lower typical bands and premium tiers to $22); retrofit acoustic panel treatment $18–$45 per square foot (acousticmod.com, "Acoustic Retrofit vs. New Construction: Cost & Time Guide," as captured in research; page since relocated). Non-airport, medium-confidence directional benchmarks; airside premiums would raise both ranges.
claim: Commercial pricing guides put new-construction acoustic ceiling treatment at roughly $5–$15 per square foot and retrofit panel treatment at roughly $18–$45.
verification_note: designtransitionstudio.com fetched 2026-08-11 (page quotes several bands including lower typical ranges; footnote discloses this). Retrofit range per the captured acousticmod.com guide; page since relocated. Both presented as directional non-airport benchmarks.

citation: Moody's projection as reported in *The Bond Buyer*, "MWAA goes to market" (2025, bondbuyer.com): net revenue debt-service coverage declining from 1.63× in 2024 to around 1.3× over the next five years; approximately $5.5 billion of new debt planned 2025–2028; adjusted debt per O&D enplanement peaking near $400 in 2028 versus $223 in 2024. Underlying rating-agency reports are the primary citation-grade source.
claim: Moody's projects debt-service coverage compressing from 1.63× in 2024 to roughly 1.3× over five years as approximately $5.5 billion of new debt phases in,
verification_note: Bond Buyer article fetched 2026-08-11: 1.63x (2024) declining to ~1.3x, $5.5B new debt 2025-2028 confirmed.

citation: *Respiratory Therapy Magazine*, "Alarm Fatigue in Adult ICU" (respiratory-therapy.com): reviews the alarm-fatigue literature underlying clinical alarm-management policy, including a large academic medical center logging 74,535 alarms across eight units in one week. Reported per-bed figures vary by study; used as illustrative magnitude, not a universal baseline.
claim: In the alarm-fatigue studies the Joint Commission cites, monitored units log alarm counts that run to thousands a day across a floor — and clinicians had stopped hearing them.
verification_note: Cited article fetched 2026-08-11; a specific per-bed figure in the research base could not be located in the article, so the draft states magnitude only and the footnote reports the article's own count.

citation: The Joint Commission, National Patient Safety Goal NPSG.06.01.01, *Clinical Alarm Management*, effective January 1, 2014 (phase one), January 1, 2016 (phase two).
claim: It was National Patient Safety Goal NPSG.06.01.01, phased in 2014 and 2016: every accredited hospital had to inventory its alarms, rank them, govern them, and prove it.
verification_note: Joint Commission NPSG identity and phase dates confirmed in fact-check pass.

citation: MWAA 2025 traffic reporting: approximately 29.01 million passengers at IAD, 10.53 million of them international, the highest 2025 growth among the fifty largest U.S. airports. claim: IAD moved 29.01 million passengers in 2025, 10.53 million of them international — the fastest 2025 growth among the fifty largest US airports.

verification_note: crankyflier.com article confirmed in fact-check pass; presented as attributed analyst commentary.

citation: London City Airport, silent-airport policy implemented 2008; no flight or gate announcements since August 18, 2016, except essential and emergency (londoncityairport.com).
claim: London City has run a silent policy since 2008.
verification_note: Confirmed via search in fact-check pass (primary page returned 403).

citation: Helsinki-Vantaa (Finavia, silent regime since 2015, gate-area and emergency overrides retained); Copenhagen Airport operator-published passenger-communication policy; Amsterdam Schiphol, operator-described "Silent Airport" model with information on screens and airport app. No published intelligibility or missed-boarding measurement identified for any of these airports in this research pass.
claim: Helsinki-Vantaa, silent since 2015, and Copenhagen moved information to screens and apps.
verification_note: Helsinki 2015 start confirmed across sources in fact-check pass.

citation: San Francisco International Airport, Quiet Airport program outcomes as reported in trade press citing SFO: individual paging occurrences 492 to 261 per day; cumulative paging duration 145 to 58 minutes per day. claim: SFO reports its Quiet Airport program cut individual paging from 492 to 261 occurrences per day and cumulative announcement time from 145 to 58 minutes.
verification_note: Trade-press articles reporting SFO's own figures confirmed in fact-check pass; attributed to SFO in the draft.

citation: *Simple Flying*, "Why This Airport's 'Quiet Policy' Is Frustrating Some Passengers" (simpleflying.com): contemporaneous accounts documenting missed-flight incidents and confusion attributed to SFO's reduced-announcement practice.
claim: The same record holds documented passenger complaints and missed-flight anecdotes.
verification_note: Simple Flying article confirmed in fact-check pass.

citation: 28 C.F.R. § 35.160 (Title II of the Americans with Disabilities Act): effective communication; auxiliary aids and services. See "ADA Requirements: Effective Communication" (ada.gov).
claim: obligates MWAA to ensure effective communication with people with disabilities.
verification_note: Federal regulation; confirmed against ada.gov in fact-check pass.

citation: U.S. Department of Justice, *2010 ADA Standards for Accessible Design*, §§ 219 and 706: assistive-listening systems required in assembly areas where audible communication is integral to use.
claim: The 2010 ADA Standards §219 and §706 require assistive-listening systems in each assembly area where audible communication is integral to use.
verification_note: Federal standards; confirmed against DOJ/Access Board in fact-check pass.

citation: 14 C.F.R. Part 382 (Air Carrier Access Act implementing regulations, ecfr.gov): carriers must make facilities and services accessible, including prompt access for passengers needing visual or hearing assistance to the same gate information provided to other passengers.
claim: Under 14 CFR Part 382, passengers who need visual or hearing assistance must receive prompt access to the same trip information other passengers get at the gate.
verification_note: Federal regulation quoted from eCFR in the research base; sentence rewritten in remediation to the provision the evidence record actually documents.

citation: Airport Cooperative Research Program, *ACRP Research Report 239: Assessing Airport Programs for Travelers with Disabilities and Older Adults* (Transportation Research Board, 2023): treats digital and app channels as complements rather than substitutes for staffed and audio communication.
claim: ACRP Research Report 239 treats digital-first substitution as partial, not sufficient, for travelers with disabilities and older adults.
verification_note: Report identity confirmed against the ACRP catalog in fact-check pass; chapter text not directly rendered.

citation: IEC 60268-16:2020 scope: the standard does not cover the case of fluctuating noise on the Speech Transmission Index (general comments in §7.13 and §8.9.3). MWAA specification should therefore require commissioning verification under representative operating traffic in addition to an empty-building baseline, treated as verification-with-cure-period rather than an occupancy condition.
claim: the standard itself does not cover fluctuating background noise, which is exactly why an empty-building reading is not a commissioning result;
verification_note: IEC scope statement (§7.13, §8.9.3) quoted in the research base from the IEC webstore listing.

citation: 29 C.F.R. § 1910.95 (OSHA, Occupational Noise Exposure): hearing-conservation program required at 85 dB(A) eight-hour time-weighted average.
claim: a hearing conservation program per 29 CFR 1910.95, occupational noise exposure;
verification_note: Federal regulation; confirmed against osha.gov in fact-check pass.
